1282.title: Sakya
1282.hook: the school of the gray earth, led by the Khon family
1282.howItsDone: Sakya Buddhists study and practice in monasteries and centers of the Sakya school, honoring the Sakya Trizin as the head of the tradition and the Khon family as its historic holders.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three-year retreat: three years and three fortnights of practice behind a closed door, kept by Kagyu and other schools. A new week starts now.

A hillside in southern Tibet, and the soil on it is pale. Not brown, not red: a dusty, ashy gray, the color of a cooled fire. Tradition says a man of the Khon family built a monastery on that slope, and the place took its name from the ground under it. Sakya. The gray earth. A whole school of Tibetan Buddhism is named for a patch of dirt, and for a long time one family led it, parents and children and nephews, handing the work down at home as much as from the teaching throne.
screen: `A HILLSIDE OF PALE SOIL.` → `THE KHON FAMILY BUILDS THERE.` → `A SCHOOL NAMED FOR THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Sakya is usually translated as gray earth, or pale earth, after that hillside. Plenty of schools carry a founder's name or an idea. This one is named for a place you could kneel down and touch: in this school, the teaching has an address. Second, the family. The Sakya tradition remembers the Khon family as its holders. Leadership passed down within that family, often from uncle to nephew, and the head of the school came to be called the Sakya Trizin, the holder of the Sakya throne. In some traditions authority moves by election or by finding a reborn teacher. In this one, for much of its story, it moved through a household. Third, the scholar. Out of that family came Sakya Pandita, remembered as a great learned man. He wrote on logic and on how to read the teachings carefully, and he wrote short verses of good advice about speaking, giving and choosing friends, short enough to remember. His nephew Phagpa traveled to the court of the Mongol rulers, and tradition says he devised a written script for them. A family from a gray hillside ended up teaching at the edge of an empire. Fourth, what a family carries. A lineage is usually pictured as a line of teachers. Sakya adds something warmer and messier: kitchens, inheritances, a young person who grows up knowing the teaching is the family business and has to decide whether to take it on. The teaching came down through ordinary people, who had to agree to carry it.
screen: `GRAY EARTH: A SCHOOL WITH AN ADDRESS.` · `THE KHON FAMILY HOLDS THE THRONE.` · `SAKYA PANDITA AND HIS NEPHEW PHAGPA.` · `A LINEAGE THAT IS ALSO A HOUSEHOLD.` · then, large: `THE GRAY EARTH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one family's story, your own, a friend's, or one you've only heard about, and one thing handed down in it: a recipe, a trade, a phrase, a way of praying, a stubbornness. Ask quietly who first carried it, and who chose to keep carrying it. You don't need answers; let the question rest, the way the gray earth rests under the monastery.
Sakya. The gray earth: a Tibetan school named for a pale hillside, long held by the Khon family. Today's word.
Your line: the gray earth. A teaching with an address, carried by a family. See you tomorrow.

1283.title: The path and its fruit
1283.hook: the Sakya teaching that the path and the result are joined
1283.howItsDone: In the Sakya school, Lamdre is taught by qualified teachers in formal transmissions, often over extended sessions, to students who request it and then practice its meditations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sakya, the school of the gray earth, held for generations by the Khon family. Your line was the gray earth.

An apple tree in a backyard, in early spring. No apples yet, only bare twigs and a few hard buds. Is the apple there? In one sense, obviously not: there's nothing to pick. In another sense, it's already on its way, folded into the bud, waiting on sun and water and time. The tree isn't a different thing from the fruit. It's the fruit, still happening. The Sakya school treasures a teaching built on a question close to that one: if awakening is the fruit, where is it while you're still walking the path? Its name is Lamdre, the path and its fruit.
screen: `A BARE TREE IN SPRING.` → `IS THE APPLE ALREADY THERE?` → `LAMDRE: THE PATH AND ITS FRUIT.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Lam is path. Dre is fruit, or result. Lamdre is the path together with its result, and in Sakya it is a treasured body of teaching, passed down with great care, sometimes only to those who have asked for it and prepared. Second, where it came from. The Sakya tradition traces Lamdre back to Virupa, an Indian master remembered in stories as a wild and powerful yogi. Tradition says his teaching came to Tibet and was kept by the Khon family, so the household that held the throne also held this teaching. Third, the idea itself. On plenty of journeys, the road and the destination are separate: you suffer the highway to reach the beach. Lamdre teaches that the qualities of awakening, clarity and openness, are already present in the mind as its nature, the way the apple is present in the bud. Practice doesn't manufacture them from nothing; it uncovers and ripens what is there. That's why Sakya teachers speak of the cause, the path and the result as joined, and why some speak of the round of suffering and nirvana as not finally two. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day. If the fruit only exists at the end, today is just a toll you pay to get there. If the path is already the fruit, today's patience is a piece of awakening, not a ticket to it. A small kind word isn't a down payment. It's the thing itself, in miniature.

1284.title: Gelug
1284.hook: the school of Tsongkhapa, known for monastic study and the Dalai Lamas
1284.howItsDone: Gelug monks and nuns keep monastic vows, study classical Indian Buddhist texts in the school's monasteries, debate what they study, and meditate on it; lay Gelug Buddhists often study the school's stages-of-the-path teachings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lamdre, the Sakya teaching that the path and its fruit are joined. Your line was the path is the fruit.

Yellow. If you've seen photographs of Tibetan monks in tall, crested yellow hats, curved like a rooster's comb, you've probably seen monks of one school. People sometimes call them the yellow hats. The Dalai Lama, whose face turns up in newspapers far from Tibet, comes from that same school. But the hat and the famous name are the outside. Inside is a monk who wanted the teachings studied carefully, kept cleanly and argued out loud until they were understood. His name was Tsongkhapa. His school is called Gelug.
screen: `TALL YELLOW HATS.` → `THE DALAI LAMA'S SCHOOL.` → `A MONK NAMED TSONGKHAPA.`

segments.voice: You met Tsongkhapa on day nine hundred eighty-one; today, the school that grew from him. First, the name. Gelug is usually translated as the virtuous way, or the system of virtue. Not the clever way, not the powerful way. The way of virtue, which here starts with something unglamorous: keeping your vows. Second, the founder. Tsongkhapa studied with teachers from many schools. Tradition remembers him as a man of huge learning and strict discipline, who founded the monastery of Ganden and gathered students around a simple-sounding program: keep the monastic rules carefully, study the great Indian texts carefully, and meditate on what you've understood. His followers became the Gelug school. Third, the idea he pressed hardest. Some treat study and meditation as rivals: the scholar in the library, the yogi in the cave. Tsongkhapa held them together. You reason your way into what the teachings say, especially about emptiness, until it's clear. Then you sit with that clarity until it sinks in. Careful thinking is how you know what you're meditating on. Fourth, the lamas. Over time the Gelug school became home to the line of the Dalai Lamas, and to the Panchen Lamas too, teachers whom Tibetans understand as returning life after life. That's why the school is famous. But inside the monasteries, the daily work is a robe kept properly, a text read slowly, a hard point argued until it gives. The virtuous way, as this school walks it, is mostly carefulness.

1285.title: Monastic study
1285.hook: years of study in the great monasteries, ending in the geshe degree
1285.howItsDone: In Gelug monasteries, monks memorize root texts, attend teachings on them, and debate them in the courtyard, the questioner standing and clapping, the defender seated; after years of study some are examined for the geshe degree.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gelug, the school of Tsongkhapa. Your line was the virtuous way, which turned out to mean mostly carefulness.

A courtyard in the late afternoon, full of noise. Monks in maroon robes stand over other monks who sit on the ground. The standing one throws out a question, swings his arm high, and brings his palms together in a sharp clap, stamping his foot. The seated one answers. The crowd laughs, or groans, or goes quiet. It looks almost like a sport. It is study: debate in a Tibetan monastery, how monks in these monasteries learn the texts, by being challenged out loud, day after day, for years.
screen: `A LOUD COURTYARD.` → `A QUESTION, A CLAP, A STAMP.` → `THIS IS HOW THEY STUDY.`

segments.voice: First, the places. The great monasteries of the Gelug school, Sera, Drepung and Ganden, were built as places of learning as much as places of prayer. In exile, monks re-founded them in India, and the courtyards filled with debate again. Second, what they study. The curriculum works through the classic Indian texts: the Perfection of Wisdom, the Middle Way of Nagarjuna, the Abhidharma's map of the mind, the rules of monastic life, and the logic of how anyone knows anything at all. A monk memorizes large parts of them, hears them explained, then defends them in the courtyard. Third, why debate. A teaching you only agree with stays on the surface. One you've had to defend against a sharp opponent, who claps in your face and says, so what follows from that, goes down into the bones. Some teachers explain the clap as closing the door on confusion. Debate isn't about winning; it's about finding the weak spot in your own understanding before life finds it for you. Fourth, the long finish. After years of this, some monks sit for the geshe degree, a title that, tradition says, means spiritual friend, examined in public debate before their teachers and peers. It's what's left after years of study have been tested again and again. And the point of a geshe isn't to know more than everyone. It's to be a friend who can actually explain the path to someone who needs it.

1286.title: Jonang and the Rime movement
1286.hook: smaller schools like Jonang, and the nineteenth-century movement that honored all lineages without bias
1286.howItsDone: Teachers in the Rime spirit receive and pass on teachings from several Tibetan lineages while keeping their own; Jonang monasteries continue to teach Dolpopa's view and their own practice lineages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, monastic study: the courtyard, the clap, the long road to the geshe degree. Your line was years of study.

Small things are easy to lose. A dialect only a few old people still speak. A song that only one village sings. Tibet had its big schools, Nyingma and Kagyu, Sakya and Gelug, and it would be easy to think that's the whole map. It isn't. Tibet also held smaller lineages, some with brilliant teachers and unusual ideas, some kept alive by a handful of monasteries far from the center. In eastern Tibet, a circle of teachers looked at all the lineages around them and decided not to let any of them quietly disappear. What they started is called Rime.
screen: `SMALL THINGS ARE EASY TO LOSE.` → `THE BIG SCHOOLS AREN'T THE WHOLE MAP.` → `RIME.`

segments.voice: First, one of the smaller schools: Jonang. Its great teacher Dolpopa taught a view often called empty of other. Emptiness, as earlier lessons put it, means things are empty of a fixed self of their own. Dolpopa taught that ultimate reality, the Buddha nature, is not empty of itself, only of everything that isn't it, like a clear sky, empty of clouds but not of being sky. Other Tibetan teachers argued hard against this view, and the Jonang school was pushed to the edges for a long time. It survived, and its monasteries still teach today. Second, the word. Rime, said REE-may, means without sides, or without bias. It isn't a new school. It's a way of standing toward all the schools. Third, the people. In eastern Tibet, teachers remembered as Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo and Jamgon Kongtrul traveled to receive teachings from every lineage they could find, large and small, including Jonang. Kongtrul gathered what they received into great written collections so the teachings wouldn't be lost. They didn't erase the differences; they kept each school with its own flavor and studied it on its own terms. Fourth, what without bias means. It doesn't mean every view is the same. Rime teachers still had their own home lineages and their own convictions. It means you can hold your own way firmly and still honor someone else's, receive it carefully, and want it to survive. That's harder than agreeing with everyone, and harder than dismissing them.

1287.title: Tibet's other tradition
1287.hook: Bon, Tibet's other religion, has its own teachers and practices; it is its own tradition, not a Buddhist school
1287.howItsDone: Bonpo honor Tonpa Shenrab Miwoche as their teacher, study and practice in Bon monasteries and lineages, and circle sacred sites and turn prayer wheels counterclockwise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rime: teachers who received every lineage they could find and wanted each to survive. Your line was without bias.

A pilgrim path around a holy mountain in western Tibet. The walkers move one way, keeping the mountain on their right, as Buddhists do around a stupa or a temple. Then a small group comes toward them, walking the other way, mountain on their left. They aren't lost and they aren't being rude. They're doing it correctly, by their own tradition. They are Bonpo, followers of Bon. And this whole week of Tibetan schools has been missing them, because Bon isn't a Buddhist school at all. It's Tibet's other tradition.
screen: `A PILGRIM PATH AROUND A MOUNTAIN.` → `A FEW WALK THE OTHER WAY.` → `BON: TIBET'S OTHER TRADITION.`

segments.voice: First, its own teacher. Bonpo trace their teachings not to the Buddha Shakyamuni but to their own enlightened teacher, Tonpa Shenrab Miwoche, and their tradition tells his life story, his teachings and his deeds. That's the heart of why Bon is its own tradition: its own founder, its own account of where the teachings came from. Second, its own way of moving. Bonpo circle sacred places and turn their prayer wheels counterclockwise, the opposite direction from Buddhist pilgrims. Their sacred sign is the yungdrung, a symbol of what is unchanging, turning to the left. Small details, but they mark a whole identity. Third, what looks familiar. Bon has monasteries, monks in robes, a body of scriptures, philosophical study and debate, and its own teachings on the nature of mind, including a Dzogchen tradition of its own. An outsider might file Bon under Buddhism. Bonpo themselves don't; they describe these as Bon's own teachings, held in Bon's own lineages. Fourth, how to talk about it. For a long time Bon and the Buddhist schools lived side by side in Tibet, and each shaped the other; accounts differ on how. Some older books describe Bon as only a primitive folk religion, or as a copy of Buddhism. Bonpo reject both pictures. The respectful way is the simplest: let a tradition describe itself. Bon is not a Buddhist school, not a leftover, and not a rival. It's its own tradition, with its own teacher and its own path.

1288.title: The stages of the path
1288.hook: the step-by-step path from Atisha and Tsongkhapa
1288.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhist teachers, especially in the Gelug school, teach the lamrim in order, from the preciousness of human life through renunciation to compassion and wisdom, and students meditate on each stage in turn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bon, Tibet's other tradition, with its own teacher and its own way around the mountain. Your line was its own tradition.

Where do I actually start? Six days, six doors: the gray earth of Sakya, the path and its fruit, Gelug's virtuous way, the debate courtyard, Rime, Bon. That's a lot of doors in one corridor, and somebody walking in fresh might reasonably ask: fine, but what comes first, and what comes after that? Tibetan teachers had an answer, laid out like a staircase. It's called lamrim, the stages of the path, and the next days climb it one step at a time.
screen: `WHERE DO I START?` → `SIX DOORS IN ONE WEEK.` → `LAMRIM: A STAIRCASE.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Lam is path, the same lam as in Lamdre. Rim means stages, or steps in a series. Lamrim: the path in stages, each thing in its order. Second, Atisha, whom you met on day nine hundred thirty-six. He was an Indian Buddhist master who traveled to Tibet, and there, tradition says, he was asked to write something short and clear for people confused by the many teachings arriving at once. He wrote A Lamp for the Path to Enlightenment. In it he sorts practitioners into three kinds of person: the one who looks for a good future in this round of lives, the one who wants to be free of the round altogether, and the one who wants to be free so that all beings can be free too. Each is a step, and each includes the one below it. Third, Tsongkhapa, the founder of Gelug. He opened Atisha's little lamp into a long, careful book, the Great Treatise on the Stages of the Path. Teachers of Gelug and other schools still teach from lamrim texts, so a student can see where they are on the staircase and what comes next. Fourth, why stages help. A beginner who leaps straight to the highest teaching often finds it floating with nothing under it. A staircase says: start with what this life is, then what it costs, then what you want for others. Each step is solid because of the one before, and the steps aren't left behind as you climb. They're the floor you're standing on.
